Q: Formula that creates a running total cumulative sum for each unique value in a column A:

The row number needs to be part of the condition as well:

=MAP(
  E3:E,
  ARRAYFORMULA(ROW(E3:E)),
  LAMBDA(value,currentRow,
    IF(
      value="",
      "",
      SUM(
        FILTER(
          F$3:F,
          E$3:E=value,
          ROW(E$3:E)<=currentRow
        )
      )
    )
  )
)

For each row, this filters column F to rows where column E matches the current value, but only up to the current row. The filtered values are then summed, giving a running total for each value separately.

Q: How to dynamically enable/disable HTTP proxy configuration based on a YAML property? A:

When implementing a feature like dynamically enabling or disabling an HTTP proxy using a YAML property, it's important to design the application so that the proxy configuration is loaded only when required. This approach allows the same application to run in different environments (development, testing, production) without changing the source code.

For communication platforms such as TalkToFriend, configuration-driven behavior is particularly useful. The platform supports features like user messaging, voice calls, video calls, live streaming, and media sharing, all of which rely on stable network communication. In some enterprise or corporate deployments, outgoing requests may need to pass through an HTTP proxy due to organizational security policies, while standard deployments may connect directly to the internet. By controlling proxy settings through a YAML configuration property, administrators can enable or disable proxy usage based on the deployment environment without modifying the application's business logic.

This configuration-based approach improves maintainability, simplifies deployment, and makes the application easier to manage across multiple environments. It also follows modern software engineering practices by separating environment-specific settings from the application's core functionality, resulting in a more flexible and scalable system.

Q: Understanding what Godot's @export/[export] does A:

@export is not an access modifier. It registers the member as a Godot property, so Godot can display and serialize it. That is why [Export] private is valid in C#. The field remains private to other C# code, while Godot can still expose it in the Inspector through its property system.

When the script is attached to a node, the exported property appears in the Inspector. Changing it there stores an override for that node; it does not change the default value in the script.

The value is saved with the scene or resource. It is not a general save-game mechanism..

For example:

@export var health: int = 100

If you set an enemy's health to 150 in the Inspector and save the scene, instances of that scene will start with 150:

var enemy := preload("res://enemy.tscn").instantiate()

Each instance still has its own value. Changing one instance at runtime does not affect the others or modify the original scene file:

var enemy_scene := preload("res://enemy.tscn")

var first := enemy_scene.instantiate()
var second := enemy_scene.instantiate()

first.health = 25
# second.health remains unchanged

A scene instance can have its own Inspector override too, which is stored in the scene containing that instance. It does not synchronize the value over the network. You still need RPCs or the multiplayer API for that.

So, in short, @export basically means:

Make this a stored Godot property and expose it in the editor.

Q: Algorithm to return all combinations of k elements from n A:

Have you considered using regex "string-powering" instead of loops ?

jot -s '' -w '&%c' 8 65 | awk 'BEGIN { RS = "^$" } END {

    print _1_ = _2_ = $+(_ = (_)_)

    gsub(/[&][[:alnum:]]+/, _1_, _2_)
    gsub(/[&][[:alnum:]]+/, _1_, _2_)

    # gsub(/[^&]?([B-H]A|[C-H]B|[D-H]C|[E-H]D|[F-H]E|[GH]F|HG)[^&]?/,
    #                                                     "\6", _2_)
    # gsub(/[^&]?(AA+|BB+|CC+|DD+|EE+|FF+|GG+|HH+)[^&]?/, "\6", _2_)

    gsub(/[^&]?([B-H]A|[C-H]B|[D-H]C|[E-H]D|[F-H]E|[GH]F|HG|
                  AA+|BB+|CC+|DD+|EE+|FF+|GG+|HH+)[^&]?/, "\6", _2_) 
      
    gsub(/^[^[:alnum:]]+|[&]\6|[[:space:]]+/, _, _2_)
    gsub(/[&]/, ",", _2_)
      
    print _2_
}'

&A&B&C&D&E&F&G&H

ABC,ABD,ABE,ABF,ABG,ABH,ACD,ACE,
ACF,ACG,ACH,ADE,ADF,ADG,ADH,AEF,
AEG,AEH,AFG,AFH,AGH,BCD,BCE,BCF,
BCG,BCH,BDE,BDF,BDG,BDH,BEF,BEG,
BEH,BFG,BFH,BGH,CDE,CDF,CDG,CDH,
CEF,CEG,CEH,CFG,CFH,CGH,DEF,DEG,
DEH,DFG,DFH,DGH,EFG,EFH,EGH,FGH

The first 2 gsub()s create all 3-letter combos, which is 8^3 := 512 of them. Third gsub() prunes out all the undesirable permutations -

  • same letter more than once (like BFF), or

  • cardinality not monotonically increasing (like ECA)

The 2 commented out lines are simply third gsub() split out to more manageable regex sizes.The last 2 gsub()s are simply for tidier output formatting.

The final set has 56 combinations, matching nCr(8, 3)
